idiom_name: map[string]any field plus accessor methods; json.Unmarshal into map[string]any
implementation_notes: Go has no member lookup by runtime name, so the local idiom is a plain map field with Get/Set/Remove methods; encoding/json decodes an unknown JSON object straight into map[string]any, which is how dynamic documents normally enter a Go program, while struct tags plus reflect.Type give descriptors for the fixed part. The classic owner/property-list/descriptor structure is replaced by the map plus methods - hand-written descriptor tables are worth it only when consumers must enumerate the legal keys. The map is the property list, and the method names replace the pattern's named accessors.
pitfalls: Values stored as any must be type-asserted at every read (v, ok := attrs[k].(string)); a failed assertion is the Go equivalent of the pattern's absent or wrong-type failure, and the zero value hides it if the comma-ok form is skipped.
A map is not safe for concurrent writes: concurrent writes, or a write during iteration, abort the program with a runtime fatal error that recover cannot catch - guard with a mutex or shard the map.
encoding/json decodes JSON numbers into float64 when the target is any, so large integers lose precision; use json.Decoder.UseNumber or a typed struct when identifiers matter.
reflect can only read and set exported struct fields, so reflection-driven descriptors silently skip unexported state (CanSet is false).
